facts.text: Wu-Tang Clan's Ol' Dirty Bastard borrowed this film's title for his 1995 debut solo album, Return to the 36 Chambers: The Dirty Version.
Wu-Tang Clan's '36 Chambers' tag is math: 9 members x 4 heart chambers = 36. It also nods to the first film in this series, The 36th Chamber of Shaolin (1978).
In the first and third 36th Chamber films, star Gordon Liu plays the real Shaolin monk San Te. Here he plays Chu Jen-chieh, a small-time con man who only pretends to be one.
Screenwriter Ni Kuang wrote this film. He is credited with over 400 film scripts and 300 novels, and he fled mainland China in 1956 after escaping a ten-year sentence.
Director Lau Kar-leung was reportedly reluctant to make a 36th Chamber sequel, so he made a spoof with a comic con-artist hero instead of a straight follow-up.
Shaw Brothers' Movietown was once the largest privately owned film studio in the world, with 15 stages and 1,300 employees. This movie was made on that lot.
Yeong-moon Kwon, who plays Yuan Li-hao, was a tae kwon do instructor to both Sylvester Stallone and Muhammad Ali. He later turned up in the cult oddity Miami Connection.
Kara Hui (Hsiao Hung) got her start by luck. On Dirty Ho (1979) the lead actress quit over the stunt strain, and director Lau Kar-leung cast Hui, then an extra, after seeing her audition tape.
Kara Hui (Hsiao Hung) joined Shaw Brothers at 17 via director Chang Cheh. Lau Kar-leung's films like this one made her a kung fu heroine, and she won Best Actress for My Young Auntie.
Johnny Wang Lung-wei, who plays mill owner Boss Wang, was usually cast as the villain in his Hong Kong movie roles.
One reviewer called this film's broad slapstick, laxative gags included, 'a prototype Stephen Chow comedy, minus the irony.'
Writer Ni Kuang also wrote the screenplay for Fist of Fury (1972), the Bruce Lee classic. He wasn't credited as creator of Chen Zhen, the hero Lee played.
Hsiao Ho, who plays mill worker Ah Chao here, went on to star as folk hero Fong Sai-yuk in the series' third film, Disciples of the 36th Chamber (1985).
Gordon Liu's con man Chu Jen-chieh is given a huge chore at the Shaolin temple: build scaffolding around the whole complex. It takes him more than a year, and it becomes his secret kung fu training.
Star Gordon Liu later played two roles in Kill Bill: yakuza bodyguard Johnny Mo in Vol. 1 and the cruel kung fu master Pai Mei in Vol. 2.
Hsiao Ho's funniest set mishap came on Mad Monkey Kung Fu. During an acrobatic stunt he smashed his face into the backside of a co-star.
Quentin Tarantino planned to play Pai Mei himself in Kill Bill Vol. 2, but found directing took everything he had. He gave it to Gordon Liu: 'almost criminal' not to.
Ol' Dirty Bastard's 'Return to the 36 Chambers' sold 81,000 copies its first week in 1995, peaked at #7 on the Billboard 200, and earned a Best Rap Album Grammy nomination.
Wu-Tang's Masta Killa took his name from 'Master Killer,' an alternate title of the first film. This sequel's alternate English title is Return of the Master Killer.
The first film's hero San Te was loosely based on a real 17th-century martial artist. His famous invention of the three-section staff is pure movie fiction.
Director Lau Kar-leung avoided wirework and trampolines, saying: 'My only aim in making a film is to exalt the martial arts.'
Behind-the-scenes footage from this film appears in Citizen Shaw (1980), a rare documentary about the Shaw Brothers studio.
Shaw Brothers wasn't only kung fu. The studio also invested in Western productions including Blade Runner and Meteor.
Hsiao Ho, who plays Ah Chao, said in a 2004 interview that he doesn't watch his old movies, except for Mad Monkey Kung Fu.
This sequel is much lighter in tone than the 1978 original, which disappointed some fans. Reviewers still praise its martial arts choreography.
Director Lau Kar-leung later choreographed Jackie Chan's Drunken Master II (1994). They clashed over fighting style, and he left before the final fight was shot.
One reviewer calls the third film, Disciples of the 36th Chamber (1985), the weakest of the trilogy. They still note top-notch martial arts and acrobatics.
Gordon Liu was born a different surname. Out of respect for his master Cham Lau, whose Hung Gar school trained him, he took the surname Liu (Lau in Cantonese).
Screenwriter Ni Kuang's son, Joe Nieh, is married to Hong Kong actress Vivian Chow. Ni Kuang also wrote the Wisely sci-fi novels, which became films and TV shows.
Composer Eddie Wang's 'twangy' hero theme for this film is singled out by critics as one of its musical highlights.
Kara Hui (Hsiao Hung) returned to acting in 2005 after a long career lull. She went on to win three Hong Kong Film Award Best Actress prizes and a Bronze Bauhinia Star in 2018.
The real monk San Te is played here by Lee King-chue, not by Gordon Liu, who played him in the original 1978 film.
One reviewer says this film is 'perhaps overlooked because of the comedy.' He still calls it a formidable piece of entertainment that is its own creation, not a remake of the first film.
